01.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had allowed the people of Geder, a town at the top of a slope, to go down to Hamtan on Shabbat, but did not let the people of Hamtan go up to Geder. When Rav Dimi came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, he explained the real reason: the people of Geder used to assault the people of Hamtan. So the rule was not a ruling about Shabbat limits at all but an ordinance Rabbi made to keep the peace.
01.why: Rav Yosef had cited the Geder and Hamtan rule as proof that a town on a slope measures its Shabbat limit from a barrier it builds. Rav Dimi's report takes that proof away, and the Gemara goes on to ask why such an ordinance would apply only on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported the true reason behind Rabbi's rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he permitted the people of Geder to go down to Hamtan but not the reverse.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only a set distance, two thousand cubits, beyond the place where he is staying. The discussion is about where that distance is measured from.
A rule the Sages made for the public good, as opposed to a ruling that follows from the law itself.

02.note: Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya and Rav Abba bar Tahalifa visited Rav Aha son of Rav Ika, in the town where Rav Aha bar Ya'akov was the authority. Their host wanted to slaughter a choice third-born calf for them and showed them the knife. Rav Aha bar Tahalifa asked whether they should not show it to the Elder of the town out of respect. Rabbi Elazar answered that Rava had said a Torah scholar may examine a knife for himself, and he examined it. He was later punished by Heaven.
02.why: The Gemara has just cited Rava's ruling that a Torah scholar may check a slaughtering knife himself. This story shows its limit: once the local Elder's honor had been raised, ignoring him was punished, as the Gemara goes on to explain.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya
people.about: A visiting Sage who checked the knife himself, relying on Rava's ruling, and was punished for it.

people.name: Rav Abba bar Tahalifa
people.about: His travelling companion, who asked whether they should show the knife to the town's Elder. The English also calls him Rav Aha bar Tahalifa.

people.name: Rav Aha son of Rav Ika
people.about: Their host, who wanted to slaughter a calf for them.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
people.about: The Elder, the senior authority of the town where this happened.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Rabbi Elazar cited: a Torah scholar may examine a knife for himself.

terms.meaning: A calf considered a delicacy; the translation explains its meat was prized.
A knife for ritual slaughter must be perfectly smooth, so it was customary to show it to the local Sage for inspection before use.

03.note: Ravina was sitting before his teacher Rav Ashi when he saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. He shouted at him, but the man paid no attention, and Ravina declared the man excommunicated. Afterward Ravina asked Rav Ashi whether acting like that in his presence looked disrespectful. Rav Ashi quoted the verse "There is no wisdom or understanding or counsel against the Lord": where God's name is being desecrated, no respect is paid even to a teacher.
03.why: Rava teaches that a student may not rule on law in his teacher's presence, except to stop someone doing something forbidden. Ravina's case illustrates that exception, and the discussion then turns to the punishment for a student who rules before his teacher.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A student who rebuked and excommunicated a Shabbat violator while sitting before his teacher.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ravina's teacher, who approved of what he did.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules that a student may rule in his teacher's presence to stop a transgression.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on a person by a Sage, cutting him off from normal dealings with the community until he mends his ways.
The Sages forbade making use of a growing tree on Shabbat, such as tying an animal to it.
Conduct that brings disrespect on God or His law in public view.

04.note: One of Rabbi Eliezer's students issued a legal ruling in his teacher's presence. Rabbi Eliezer said to his wife, Imma Shalom, that he would be surprised if this student lived out the year. And the student did not complete his year.
04.why: The Gemara has just cited Rabbi Eliezer's teaching that Aaron's sons died for ruling before Moses. This case backs the teaching that ruling in a teacher's presence carries a death penalty, and the Gemara then argues over how far away the student actually was.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose student ruled on law in front of him; he predicted the student would not survive the year.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife, to whom he made the prediction.

terms.term: issuing a ruling in one's teacher's presence
terms.meaning: Deciding a point of law in front of one's own teacher, which the Sages treated as a grave disrespect.
Lives until the end of the year.

05.note: A gentile named Lahman bar Ristak lived in an alleyway with Jewish neighbors. They asked him to rent them his rights in the alleyway so they could carry there on Shabbat, but he refused. They went to Abaye, who told them all to give up their rights in favor of one of them, so that a single Jew would be living with a gentile, a case where the gentile does not forbid carrying. They objected that this rule exists only because such living arrangements are rare, and here many people live there. Abaye answered that many people renouncing in favor of one is itself rare, and the Sages made no decree for rare cases.
05.why: The Gemara returns here to renting a gentile's rights for an eiruv. Abaye's advice is a way around a gentile who will not rent, and when it is reported to Rava he objects that it would make the eiruv look unnecessary.

people.name: Lahman bar Ristak
people.about: A gentile living in the alleyway who would not rent his rights to his Jewish neighbors.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the neighbors consulted, who suggested they all renounce their rights in favor of one person.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area, so they may carry objects in a common courtyard or alleyway.
A gentile neighbor cannot join an eiruv, so Jews rent his rights in the shared space from him to let them carry there.
Giving up one's rights in a shared courtyard or alleyway to another resident, leaving fewer people who need to be joined.

06.note: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua had reported Abaye's advice to Rava. Rava objected that it abolished the eiruv in that alleyway, since people would see them carrying without one. Rav Huna answered that the residents would make an eiruv anyway as a reminder. Rava said people would then think an eiruv works even where a gentile has not rented out his rights. Rav Huna said they would make a public announcement. Rava retorted: will an announcement reach the children?
06.why: This continues the case of the gentile Lahman bar Ristak, who would not rent his rights. Rava rejects Abaye's way around him and then offers his own: one neighbor should befriend the gentile and become like his hired worker.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who objected to Abaye's advice.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: He reported Abaye's advice to Rava and defended it.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area, so they may carry objects in a common courtyard or alleyway.

06.flag: Starts mid-exchange: the speaker (Rava) and the person addressed are named only in the segment before, and the story is a back-and-forth legal argument with no events of its own.

07.note: Rabban Gamliel was riding a donkey from Akko to Keziv, with his student Rabbi Elai walking behind. He found loaves of bread on the road and told Elai to pick them up, then met a gentile and said: Mavgai, take these loaves from Elai. Elai asked the man his name and whether Rabban Gamliel had ever met him. It was Mavgai, and they had never met, so they learned Rabban Gamliel had spoken by divine inspiration. At Keziv a man came to have a vow released. Rabban Gamliel confirmed with Elai that they had drunk a quarter-log of Italian wine and told the man to follow them until the wine wore off. After three mil, at the Ladder of Tyre, he got down, wrapped himself in his shawl, sat, and released the vow.
07.why: Rami bar Abba has just said that walking a mil dispels the effect of wine. This story seems to show it takes three mil, and the Gemara answers that Italian wine is stronger.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage riding to Keziv, who knew a stranger's name and later released a man's vow.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's student, walking behind him.

people.name: Mavgai
people.about: A gentile from the nearby towns of guardsmen, who was given the loaves.

terms.meaning: A Sage may dissolve a person's vow after hearing him out; the story shows he did it only sober and seated.
A small measure of liquid, roughly a large cupful.
A measure of distance, about two thousand cubits, a little under a kilometer.
A gift of insight from God; here, knowing a stranger's name without being told.

08.note: Reish Lakish and the students of Rabbi Hanina came to an inn on Shabbat. A gentile tenant there was away, but the gentile landlord was present. They wondered whether they could rent the tenant's rights from the landlord, who had the power to remove him but had not done so. Reish Lakish said: let us rent now, and ask our Sages in the South when we get there. Later they asked Rabbi Afes, who told them they had acted well.
08.why: The discussion is about when a gentile's presence forbids carrying and who can rent out his rights for an eiruv. This case asks whether a landlord can rent out a tenant's room, and the Gemara follows it with a second inn story about renting on Shabbat itself.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage travelling with the students of Rabbi Hanina, who decided they should rent and ask later.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: One of the Sages in the South, who approved what they did.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area, so they may carry objects in a common courtyard.
A gentile cannot join an eiruv, so Jews living with him rent his rights in the shared space to be allowed to carry.

09.note: Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi came to an inn, and the gentile innkeeper arrived on Shabbat. They asked whether they could rent his rights then. Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef said to rent; Rabbi Asi said not to; Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said they should rely on the Elder, Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef, and rent. Later they asked Rabbi Yohanan, who said they had acted well. The Sages of Neharde'a wondered whether Rabbi Yohanan had really said this, since he had also said that renting is like making an eiruv.
09.why: It follows a similar inn case about renting from a landlord. The Gemara then reconciles Rabbi Yohanan's two statements: renting is like an eiruv only in its leniencies, such as a tiny payment or renting from a gentile's hired worker.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef
people.about: The Elder of the group, who said they should rent.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: He said to follow the Elder and rent.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: He said they should not rent.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage they asked afterward, who said they had acted well.

people.name: Sages of Neharde'a
people.about: Scholars who questioned whether Rabbi Yohanan had really said this.

terms.meaning: An arrangement that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area for carrying on Shabbat; it must be set up before Shabbat begins.
Giving up one's rights in a shared courtyard to the other residents, which may be done even on Shabbat.

10.note: On Shabbat the warm water prepared for a baby's circumcision spilled. Rava had water in his courtyard, but had not joined his courtyard with the baby's by an eiruv. He told those who asked him to move his belongings from the men's room, which opened onto his courtyard, into the inner women's room. He would sit there and renounce his rights in his courtyard in favor of the baby's household, so the water could be carried across. The text does not say what happened next.
10.why: The Gemara is telling a run of cases about the baby whose water spilled. Ravina then asks how Rava could do this when Shmuel said rights cannot be renounced from one courtyard to another, and Rava says he follows Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who offered to give up his rights in his courtyard so the water could reach the baby.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes or courtyards into one area, so objects may be carried between them.
Giving up one's share in a courtyard to others, so that they count as its only residents and may carry there.
A baby's circumcision is done on the eighth day even when that falls on Shabbat; warm water was used to wash the baby.

11.note: Ravina pressed Rava, who planned to give up his rights in his courtyard so water could be carried to a baby. Why not stay where you are, renounce in their favor, and then have them renounce back to you, as Rav permits? Rava answered that on that point he follows Shmuel, who forbids renouncing back and forth. Ravina objected that Shmuel's reason is the same one that forbids renouncing from one courtyard to another, which Rava was doing. Rava replied that Shmuel's reason is different: renouncing back and forth would make the words of the Sages a laughingstock.
11.why: The Gemara then takes up Rav and Shmuel's dispute over renouncing and renouncing back, and asks whether it matches an older disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: He questioned Rava's plan and its consistency.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He planned to renounce his courtyard rights for a baby's sake and defended his reasoning.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage quoted as allowing one resident to renounce to another and then receive the rights back.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage quoted as forbidding that back-and-forth renouncing.

terms.meaning: Giving up one's share in a shared courtyard to others for Shabbat, so they may carry there without an eiruv.
A respectful way of addressing a Sage; here Ravina means Rava.

11.flag: Starts mid-sentence (Ravina's question begins in the segment before) and is a legal argument continuing the spilled-water story rather than a new story.

12.note: Rabban Gamliel recalled a Sadducee who lived in the same alleyway in Jerusalem as his family and had given up his rights in it before Shabbat. His father told them to hurry and take their utensils out into the alleyway before the Sadducee took his out and forbade it to them. In a version taught by Rabbi Meir, Rabban Gamliel told his sons to hurry and carry what they needed before that loathsome man took out his things. Rabbi Yehuda reports his words differently: hurry and do what you need in the alleyway before night falls.
12.why: The mishna asks whether a Sadducee, who rejects the Sages' traditions, counts as a gentile for an eiruv. The Gemara says Rabban Gamliel told this incident to show he does not, and then works through Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yehuda's versions.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: He tells of a Sadducee who shared his family's alleyway; in one version he urges his sons to hurry.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose version of Rabban Gamliel's words is quoted first.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: He gives a different version of what Rabban Gamliel said.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group that rejected the Sages' oral traditions.
A member of a group close to the Sadducees, likewise rejecting the Sages' traditions.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
Gave up his share in the shared alleyway so the others could carry there on Shabbat.

13.note: A man went out into the public street on Shabbat wearing a coral ring, which is forbidden. When he saw Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, he covered it. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said that someone like this may renounce his rights in a courtyard, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
13.why: The Gemara has just said, following Rabbi Yehuda, that only a Jew who breaks Shabbat brazenly in public is barred from renouncing his rights. A man who hides his transgression shows who falls on the other side of that line.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The Sage the man saw; he judged that the man may still renounce his rights.

terms.meaning: Give up his share in a shared courtyard so his neighbors may carry there on Shabbat. A Jew who openly breaks Shabbat is treated like a gentile and cannot do this.
Wearing such an ornament into the public domain on Shabbat counts as carrying it, which is forbidden.

14.note: Ivut bar Ihi lived in an alleyway that had only one house and one courtyard. He put up a side post for it, and Shmuel permitted him to carry there. Later Rav Anan came and threw the side post down. Ivut bar Ihi said with resentment: shall Rav Anan bar Rav come and throw it down from the alleyway where I have been living and walking by Master Shmuel's ruling?
14.why: When Rabbi Elazar challenged Shmuel's ruling that such an alleyway can be permitted with a side post, Shmuel fell silent. The Gemara uses this story to argue he never retracted, then rejects the proof: a synagogue attendant slept there, so the alley had two residences.

people.name: Ivut bar Ihi
people.about: A man who lived in the alleyway and put up a side post on Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who permitted Ivut to carry in his alleyway.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Also called Rav Anan bar Rav; he came and threw the side post down.

terms.meaning: A post set up at the open end of an alleyway that marks it off so residents may carry within it on Shabbat. Normally it works only for an alleyway with at least two courtyards.

15.note: Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law went to a bathhouse beyond the Shabbat limit before Shabbat, and it grew dark before she could return. Her mother-in-law set up an eiruv for her so she could come home. The case came before Rabbi Hiyya, who forbade it. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei said to him: Babylonian, are you so strict about eiruv? My father said, wherever you can be lenient with eiruv, be lenient. The Sages later asked why it had been invalid. Rabbi Ya'akov, sent by Rabbi Zeira to ask Rav Ya'akov bar Idi, was told it was the mother-in-law's food and she had not given her daughter-in-law ownership of it.
15.why: Rav holds that food for a Shabbat-limit eiruv must be formally given to the people it serves. The Gemara says this is an old dispute and cites Rabbi Hiyya's ruling in this case as Rav's source.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: His daughter-in-law was caught outside the Shabbat limit.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who ruled the mother-in-law's eiruv invalid.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: He rebuked Rabbi Hiyya for being too strict, quoting his father.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov
people.about: Also called son of the daughter of Ya'akov; he reported Rabbi Yohanan's explanation and was sent to ask Rav Ya'akov bar Idi.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage at the Ladder of Tyre who explained why the eiruv had failed.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only two thousand cubits beyond the place where he is staying.
A kind of eiruv: food placed before Shabbat at a spot that then counts as one's home base, letting one walk further from there.
Formally giving the eiruv food to the people it is meant for, usually through someone who receives it on their behalf.

16.note: The son of Bonyas, a very rich man, came before Rabbi, who told his attendants: make way for one worth a hundred maneh. Another man came, and Rabbi said: make way for one worth two hundred maneh. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei said: Rabbi, this one's father has a thousand ships at sea and a thousand towns on land. Rabbi answered: when you reach his father, tell him not to send him to me in these clothes. The Gemara comments that Rabbi and Rabbi Akiva both honored the wealthy.
16.why: The mishna's "right of usage" was just explained by the courtyard of Bonyas, a rich man who kept his goods in his tenants' rooms. The Gemara adds this second Bonyas story before going back to the law.

people.name: son of Bonyas
people.about: Son of an extremely wealthy man; he came before Rabbi in clothes that did not show his wealth.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who seated his visitors by their apparent wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: He told Rabbi how rich the young man's father was.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Mentioned by the Gemara as another Sage who honored the wealthy.

terms.meaning: A large sum of money, one hundred zuz; a hundred maneh means great wealth.

17.note: Rav Dimi reported an incident in Tzippori. The people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat. The next day they spread a sheet over the pillars between the house where the scroll was kept and the synagogue, brought the scroll through, and read from it. The Gemara at once questions this telling: may one spread a sheet on Shabbat, when everyone agrees a temporary tent may not be put up then?
17.why: The Gemara is asking whether Rabbi Yosei relied on hanging partitions for carrying on Shabbat. It says the Tzippori incident followed his son, Rabbi Yishmael, not him, and then rereads it as sheets that were already spread.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage on whose authority the Gemara says the Tzippori incident was done.

terms.meaning: A wall that hangs down without reaching the ground, such as a sheet; the question is whether it counts as a real wall for carrying on Shabbat.
Putting up any covering on Shabbat, even a temporary one, counts as building and is forbidden.

18.note: Rabbi recalled that when he and others studied Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and a towel from roof to roof, roof to courtyard, courtyard to courtyard and through enclosures until they reached the spring where they bathed. Rabbi Yehuda told of a time of danger when they carried a Torah scroll from courtyard to roof, roof to courtyard and courtyard to enclosure, in order to read from it.
18.why: Rav Yehuda has just set out the views of Rabbi Meir, the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon on carrying between roofs, courtyards and enclosures. These memories support his reading of Rabbi Shimon; the Sages answer that a time of danger proves nothing.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, recalling what he and his fellow students did while studying with Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The teacher in Tekoa with whom they studied.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who told of carrying a Torah scroll in a time of danger.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Named in the teaching on roofs, which sets out his view.

terms.meaning: A fenced area such as a yard or storage lot that is not lived in; it has its own rules for carrying on Shabbat.
A period, the translation explains, when decrees banned religious practice.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

19.note: Rav and Shmuel were sitting in a courtyard on Shabbat when the wall between it and the next courtyard fell. Shmuel told the people to take a cloak and hang it on what was left of the wall. Rav turned his face away. Shmuel said to them, joking: if Abba is particular, take his belt and tie it on.
19.why: The Gemara says Rav's view, that carrying is limited to four cubits once such a wall falls, was never stated outright but inferred from his turning away here. It then asks why Shmuel needed the cloak and why Rav stayed silent.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Also called Abba; he turned his face away when Shmuel told people to hang the cloak.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: His colleague, who told the people to hang a cloak where the wall had fallen; it was his town.

terms.meaning: Where carrying is not permitted, a person may still move an object within four cubits, about two meters.

20.note: Rabbi Meir said one may not open a door from one kind of area into another unless one has built a partition ten handbreadths high. The Rabbis answered with an incident from the poultry dealers' market in Jerusalem. The dealers would lock their shops and leave the key in a window above the door. Rabbi Yosei says it was the wool dealers' market.
20.why: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis could answer Rabbi Meir, who spoke of the public domain, with a Jerusalem market, since Jerusalem had only lesser status. Rava reads this part of the mishna as being about the gates of a garden.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who required a partition before one could open such a door.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: He says the market in question was that of the wool dealers.

terms.meaning: A measure of about 8 to 10 centimeters; ten handbreadths high is the height that makes a separate area in Shabbat law.
An in-between area, neither fully private nor fully public, where the Sages forbade carrying.

20.flag: Starts mid-sentence with the end of Rabbi Meir's ruling; the incident itself is only two lines.
